answer.label: Louisa May Alcott's own words, from Little Women (1869)
answer.sourceLine: The line is from Jo's poem “In the Garret” in Little Women, Part Two (1869), Chapter 46 (“Under the Umbrella”), where Professor Bhaer produces one of Jo's published verses. Alcott's text prints a comma after “worthy” — “Be worthy, love, and love will come” — which the popular one-liner drops.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Confirmed in Alcott's text (poem “In the Garret”)
Jo's poem “In the Garret”, Part Two, Ch. 46, “Under the Umbrella”

source.excerpt:
Half-writ poems, stories wild,
April letters, warm and cold,
Diaries of a wilful child,
Hints of a woman early old,
A woman in a lonely home,
Hearing, like a sad refrain—
“Be worthy, love, and love will come,”
In the falling summer rain.
trail: The line circulates widely as a Louisa May Alcott quote on sites like Goodreads ↗, tagged “Little Women” — and that attribution is correct.
It is a couplet from a poem, “In the Garret,” that Alcott gives to Jo in Part Two, Chapter 46 ↗ (“Under the Umbrella”), the chapter in which Professor Bhaer produces Jo's published verses.
A full-text check of the Project Gutenberg edition ↗ of Little Women finds the line verbatim in that poem: “Be worthy, love, and love will come,” in the falling summer rain.
The only difference from the popular version is punctuation: Alcott's text places a comma after “worthy,” which the tidy one-liner drops. The wording and the attribution are otherwise Alcott's own.
source.excerptNote: This is the closing stanza of Jo's poem “In the Garret” in Little Women. The familiar one-liner being checked here — “Be worthy love, and love will come” — is Alcott's own; her text simply prints a comma after “worthy.”

author.bio: Louisa May Alcott was an American novelist best known for Little Women (1868–69), a semi-autobiographical story of the four March sisters that became one of the most enduring works of American children's literature. She wrote extensively about self-improvement, work, and family life, and filled the novel with quotable lines about love and self-worth — including the verse this page traces.

items.why: These sites credit the line to Louisa May Alcott ↗ and tag it “Little Women” — and they are right: it is Jo's verse in Part Two, Chapter 46.
Alcott's text reads “Be worthy, love, and love will come,” with a comma after “worthy”; the popular one-liner simply drops it. The words themselves are unchanged.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: For over 150 years, Little Women has supplied readers with genuine lines about love, ambition, and self-worth. This is one of them: a couplet from a poem Alcott gives to Jo, the aspiring writer, in the chapter where Professor Bhaer finally reads her published verses.

This particular line has circulated for years on quote-collection sites, attached to Alcott and to Little Women — and the attribution checks out. A search of the novel's full text turns it up verbatim in the poem “In the Garret,” differing from the popular version only by a comma.
context.pull: Jo's own verse, tucked into a garret poem — quoted ever since, almost to the comma.
